body:
Meaning and purpose of science communication

Science communication is the process of explaining scientific knowledge, evidence, methods, applications and limitations to different audiences. It connects scientific work with the decisions people make in everyday life.

Scientists may communicate with other researchers through publications and conferences. Teachers explain scientific ideas to students. Health workers, agricultural officers and public authorities communicate scientific information to communities. In each case, the explanation must be accurate, understandable and appropriate to the audience.

Effective science communication does more than announce a conclusion. It explains what is known, how it is known, how reliable the evidence is and what remains uncertain. Its purpose is to help people make informed decisions rather than simply accept a statement because it comes from an expert.

Scientific temper is an attitude of questioning, examining evidence, using reason and remaining willing to revise a belief when reliable new evidence appears.

From observation to scientific explanation

An observation is something noticed or measured. An inference is an explanation or conclusion drawn from observations. An inference may be reasonable without yet being established as a fact.

For example, a person who develops a cough has an observable symptom. However, a cough may have several causes. The symptom alone cannot establish which disease, if any, is responsible. A reliable medical explanation requires additional evidence, such as clinical examination and appropriate investigations.

The same distinction applies outside medicine. Water that appears clear is not necessarily safe to drink. Its appearance is an observation, while its safety is a separate claim requiring suitable evidence.

What makes scientific evidence stronger?

  • Systematic observation: Information is collected carefully rather than selected only because it supports a preferred belief.
  • Appropriate testing: A proposed explanation is examined using methods capable of distinguishing it from other explanations.
  • Repeatability: Comparable observations or tests can produce consistent findings under similar conditions.
  • Independent examination: Other qualified researchers can assess the evidence, methods and conclusions.
  • Consistency with wider evidence: A conclusion becomes more dependable when several reliable findings support it.

Peer review means that other specialists examine research before publication or as part of its scientific evaluation. It helps identify weaknesses but does not guarantee that every published conclusion is correct. Scientific knowledge can improve when new results reveal errors or limitations in earlier work.

Communicating a conclusion without changing its meaning

Scientific language may contain unfamiliar terms. A good explanation replaces unnecessary technical words with clear language while retaining the important conditions and limitations of the finding.

Suppose a study finds that an intervention helped people with a particular condition under specified circumstances. The accurate public message describes that benefit and those circumstances. It should not claim that the intervention works for everyone or cures every related condition.

Numbers also need context. A reported increase or decrease should identify what was measured, the period considered and the group studied. A measurement without its unit or a percentage without a clear reference group can mislead readers.

Simplification is not the same as exaggeration. A simple explanation preserves the original evidence. An exaggerated explanation makes a broader or more certain claim than the evidence supports.

Scientific information in everyday decisions

Science communication helps people understand safe drinking water, disease prevention, weather warnings, agricultural practices and the benefits and limitations of new technologies. It is especially important when information affects personal safety or public health.

Scientific understanding can also correct social myths. For example, explanations of human reproduction show why biological facts cannot be replaced by unfounded beliefs about menstruation or responsibility for the sex of a child.

Prelims focus

  • Science communication explains scientific findings, supporting evidence and limitations to an audience.
  • An observation and an inference are not identical: the inference interprets what has been observed.
  • Repeatable findings and independent examination strengthen scientific evidence.
  • Peer review helps assess research but does not guarantee that a conclusion is correct.
  • Trap: A symptom, observation or expert statement by itself is not necessarily proof of a particular cause.

[Sources: NCERT, Science, Class 6, Chapter 10, Motion and Measurement of Distances, printed pp. 97–98; NCERT, Science, Class 8, Chapter 10, Reaching the Age of Adolescence, section Myths, Taboos, Do's and Don'ts, printed p. 122; NCERT, Science, Class 9, Chapter 13, Why Do We Fall Ill?, sections 13.1–13.2, printed pp. 176–179; Indian Council of Medical Research, National Ethical Guidelines for Biomedical and Health Research Involving Human Participants, 2017, section 3.5.2, Peer Review.]

title: Science Communication: Explaining Evidence Clearly

body:
Why false scientific claims matter

Scientific claims can influence decisions about medicines, vaccination, food, agriculture, environmental hazards and public safety. Incorrect information in these areas can cause harm even when the person sharing it has good intentions.

A false claim may spread through personal conversations, social media, advertisements, videos or messages presented as official notices. Rapid sharing can make a claim appear widely accepted without making it scientifically reliable.

Misinformation and disinformation

Misinformation is false information shared without an intention to mislead. Disinformation is false information deliberately created or spread by someone who knows it is false and intends to deceive.

TermIntentionExample
MisinformationThe person shares false information without intending to deceive.A relative sincerely forwards an incorrect home-remedy claim, believing it will help others.
DisinformationThe person knowingly spreads false information to deceive.A seller knowingly invents a medical endorsement to persuade people to buy an ineffective product.

The key distinction is knowledge and intention, not simply whether the claim is false. The intention of a person who forwarded a message usually cannot be established from the message alone.

Information can also mislead without being entirely fabricated. An old report may be circulated as a current finding. A statement may omit an important condition. A graph may use a misleading scale. A finding about a limited group may be presented as applicable to the whole population.

Common warning signs

The following features justify closer examination, although none proves by itself that a claim is false:

  • Untraceable source: The message names no study, agency, author or original document.
  • Appeal to authority without evidence: It claims endorsement by a scientist, hospital or government body but provides no verifiable record.
  • Absolute language: It promises a guaranteed cure or claims that a method has no risks under any circumstances.
  • Selective evidence: It cites only favourable examples while ignoring relevant contrary findings or limitations.
  • Missing context: A number appears without a date, population, measurement method or meaningful comparison.
  • Pressure to share immediately: The message urges forwarding before the information has been checked.

Anecdotes, association and causation

An anecdote is an account of an individual experience. It may suggest something worth investigating, but it does not necessarily establish what caused the event.

Association means that 2 events or characteristics occur together or show a relationship. Causation means that one factor produces an effect. An association alone does not prove causation because other explanations may exist.

For example, an adverse event following immunization (AEFI) is an undesirable medical occurrence after vaccination. The fact that an event occurred after vaccination does not, by itself, establish that the vaccine caused it. A causality assessment examines the relevant evidence. Equally, an event should not be dismissed without appropriate examination merely because the cause is uncertain.

How to verify a scientific claim

  1. Identify the precise claim. Separate the actual statement from emotional language or personal opinions.
  2. Trace the original source. Look for the original research, official notice or authoritative explanation rather than relying only on a screenshot.
  3. Check the date and context. Establish whether the information is current and which population or situation it concerns.
  4. Examine the evidence. Determine whether the conclusion is supported by relevant observations, testing and reliable comparisons.
  5. Compare with trustworthy sources. Consult relevant scientific institutions or responsible public authorities, particularly for health and safety advice.
  6. Decide whether to share. If reliable verification is unavailable, avoid presenting the claim as established fact. Correct an earlier message when credible contrary evidence emerges.

What should be done with a doubtful message?

Suppose a viral message claims that a particular food prevents every infectious disease. A careful reader should look for the original evidence and examine whether it supports such a broad conclusion. General nutritional benefits, even if established, would not automatically prove protection against every infection.

If the statement cannot be supported, the responsible response is to withhold it or explain clearly why the evidence is insufficient. Correcting misinformation should focus on the claim and the evidence rather than humiliating the person who shared it.

Prelims focus

  • Misinformation involves false information shared without an intention to deceive.
  • Disinformation involves knowing and deliberate deception.
  • An anecdote may suggest a possible explanation but does not establish causation.
  • Association and causation are different concepts.
  • An AEFI is an event occurring after immunization; a causal link is not automatically established.
  • Trap: A widely forwarded claim does not become reliable merely because many people have seen it.

[Sources: World Health Organization, Disinformation and Public Health, questions on misinformation and disinformation, 6 February 2024, consulted 3 November 2026; World Health Organization, Global Advisory Committee on Vaccine Safety, Serious AEFI, section on causality assessment, report published 19 January 2018, consulted 3 November 2026; NCERT, Science, Class 9, Chapter 13, Why Do We Fall Ill?, sections 13.2.1 and 13.2.4, printed pp. 178–179.]

pictures.alt: Five verification steps lead to a decision: share accurately, correct the claim, or withhold it when verification is insufficient.
pictures.caption: Verification turns an unsupported claim into a reasoned decision about whether it should be shared.

title: Misinformation and Disinformation: How to Recognise Misleading Scientific Claims

body:
Why scientific conclusions may contain uncertainty

Scientific uncertainty means that available evidence does not establish every aspect of a question with complete confidence. Uncertainty can arise from limited observations, measurement limitations, natural variation or incomplete understanding of the processes involved.

Uncertainty does not automatically mean that scientists know nothing or that a conclusion is unreliable. Scientists may have strong evidence for a general pattern while remaining uncertain about its exact timing, location or effects in a particular case.

For example, meteorologists may identify conditions favourable for a cyclone and issue a warning while the precise future path remains uncertain. The warning communicates an important risk; it is not a claim that every detail of the forecast is certain.

Distinguishing a hazard from a risk

A hazard is a possible source of harm, such as a cyclone, infectious disease or hazardous chemical. Risk concerns the possibility of harm occurring, taking account of the hazard and the circumstances in which people or property are exposed to it.

The same cyclone may pose different risks to people living in vulnerable coastal settlements and people living in well-protected locations farther inland. Differences in exposure, preparedness and vulnerability influence the consequences.

Hazard and risk are related but not identical. A hazard identifies a potential source of harm. Risk concerns the possibility and consequences of that harm under particular conditions.

How to explain uncertainty accurately

Responsible communication distinguishes among established findings, likely outcomes and possibilities that are still being assessed.

ExpressionMeaningAppropriate use
EstablishedThe conclusion has strong supporting evidence within its stated conditions.For a well-supported scientific principle.
LikelyCurrent evidence supports an outcome, but it is not certain.For a supported forecast or expectation.
PossibleAn outcome may occur, but its occurrence has not been established.For a plausible but uncertain outcome.
Not yet knownThe available information is insufficient to determine the answer.When a claim cannot presently be resolved.

These expressions should reflect the strength of the evidence. Using certain for an uncertain outcome is misleading. However, describing a strongly supported finding as completely unknown can also distort scientific understanding.

When new evidence changes an earlier conclusion, authorities should explain what changed and why. A revised forecast or recommendation is not automatically proof that the earlier communication was dishonest.

Risk communication during emergencies

Risk communication is the timely exchange of information, advice and opinions between experts or officials and people who face a possible threat. Its purpose is to help people make informed decisions and take suitable protective action.

Risk communication is two-way. Authorities provide evidence and guidance, but they must also listen to community concerns, local knowledge, practical difficulties and rumours. A warning that people cannot understand or act upon may fail even when the science behind it is sound.

What an effective warning contains

  • What is known: The observed danger or the finding supported by current evidence.
  • What is uncertain: The aspects that cannot yet be predicted or confirmed reliably.
  • What people should do: Clear, practical precautions appropriate to the threat.
  • What happens next: Where updated official information will be available and how guidance may change.

Example: a cyclone warning for coastal communities

The India Meteorological Department uses scientific observations and forecasting systems to communicate cyclone-related hazards. Satellites and radar contribute to cyclone monitoring, while official warnings support preparedness.

If a coastal area faces a possible cyclone impact, a clear message should identify the threatened area, explain uncertainty in the forecast, provide appropriate protective guidance and direct people to updated official warnings. Residents should not wait for complete certainty before following an applicable official safety instruction.

At the same time, communicators must avoid presenting a possible impact as an event that has already occurred. Clear distinctions between observation, forecast and instruction prevent unnecessary confusion.

An effective public warning must be both scientifically accurate and actionable. Suppressing uncertainty can damage trust, while giving uncertainty without practical guidance may leave people unable to respond.

Prelims focus

  • Scientific uncertainty reflects limits in available evidence, measurement or prediction.
  • A forecast may be useful even when its precise outcome remains uncertain.
  • A hazard is a potential source of harm; risk depends on the possibility and consequences of exposure.
  • Risk communication involves a two-way exchange between authorities and affected people.
  • Effective warnings explain known facts, remaining uncertainty, protective action and updates.
  • Trap: A forecast is not identical to an observation of an event that has already happened.

[Sources: World Health Organization, Emergencies: Risk Communication, questions on meaning, purpose and practice, 15 January 2020, consulted 3 November 2026; World Health Organization, Risk Communication and Community Engagement, overview, consulted 3 November 2026; NCERT, Science, Class 7, Chapter 8, Winds, Storms and Cyclones, sections 8.6–8.8, printed pp. 88–91.]
